reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of lysosomal alpha-D-mannosidase, leading to accumulation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides
Core triad comprises intellectual disability, sensorineural hearing loss, and skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex)
Coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, and recurrent infections due to immune dysfunction are common
Presentation ranges from a severe rapidly progressive infantile form to a milder form with survival into adulthood
Psychiatric symptoms and episodes of confusion can emerge in adolescents and adults
Urinary oligosaccharide screening shows a mannose-rich pattern rather than glycosaminoglycans
Diagnosis is confirmed by deficient alpha-mannosidase activity and MAN2B1 gene testing; enzyme replacement therapy is available
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha-mannosidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in MAN2B1, encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha-D-mannosidase. This enzyme cleaves terminal mannose residues during the ordered degradation of N-linked glycoproteins. Its deficiency causes accumulation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides within lysosomes throughout the body and their excretion in the urine. Storage affects the central nervous system, producing cognitive impairment; the inner ear, causing sensorineural deafness; the skeleton, causing dysostosis multiplex; and the immune system, contributing to recurrent infections. The severity spectrum reflects residual enzyme activity. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other oligosaccharidoses such as beta-mannosidosis and fucosidosis
Mucopolysaccharidoses with coarse facies and dysostosis multiplex
Other causes of intellectual disability with hearing loss and skeletal dysplasia
additionalInvestigations: Leucocyte or fibroblast alpha-mannosidase enzyme assay
Urinary oligosaccharide analysis showing mannose-rich compounds
Audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
redFlags: Recurrent severe infections indicating immune dysfunction
Cervical spine instability with cord compression
Acute confusional episodes in adolescents or adults
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; severe infantile disease progresses rapidly, whereas milder forms allow survival into adulthood with progressive cognitive, sensory, and skeletal disability. Enzyme replacement therapy is available and may improve some manifestations, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been used in selected patients.
pitfalls: Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern
Attributing recurrent infections to unrelated causes rather than the underlying disorder
Overlooking hearing loss as a key diagnostic clue
Failing to consider the diagnosis in adults presenting with new psychiatric symptoms
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Enzyme replacement therapy with velmanase alfa is the specific disease-directed treatment for non-neurological manifestations
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly in early disease, to modify progression
Provide audiological management with hearing aids or cochlear implants for sensorineural hearing loss
Treat recurrent infections promptly and maintain immunisation given the immune dysfunction
Support development, mobility and skeletal complications of dysostosis multiplex with physiotherapy, orthopaedic input and educational support
Monitor for and manage psychiatric symptoms and episodes of confusion emerging in adolescence and adulthood
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic care and offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
